about: LAWS0001 is the compulsory 30-credit first-year contract module for UCL Laws undergraduates (FHEQ Level 4), taught in person across Terms 1 and 2. It follows a contract through its life cycle: formation, interpretation, the courts' control of unfair terms, vitiating factors, frustration, and breach and remedies, while drawing out tensions in the doctrine and preparing students for both problem and essay questions. For 2026/27 it is assessed 50% by examination and 50% by coursework. This pack follows the official sequence, splitting formation and vitiating factors into two topics each.
topics: Formation: consideration, promissory estoppel and intention to create legal relations
Judicial control of unfair terms: exemption clauses, UCTA 1977, CRA 2015 and penalties
Vitiating factors: duress, undue influence and unconscionable bargains

notes.body:
A contract needs agreement, consideration, an intention to create legal relations and sufficiently certain terms. This note covers agreement and certainty.

The objective test
English law asks what a reasonable person in the position of the other party would have understood, not what a party privately intended (Smith v Hughes (1871)). The usual tool is to look for an offer that is matched by an acceptance, although the courts accept that some deals do not fit this analysis neatly (Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294).

Offer versus invitation to treat
An offer is a statement of the terms on which the offeror is willing to be bound as soon as the offeree accepts. An invitation to treat merely invites offers.
- Goods on supermarket shelves: invitation to treat; the customer offers at the till (Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists [1953] 1 QB 401).
- Goods in a shop window: invitation to treat (Fisher v Bell [1961] 1 QB 394).
- Newspaper adverts for sale: usually invitations to treat (Partridge v Crittenden [1968] 1 WLR 1204).
- Gibson: a council letter saying it "may be prepared to sell" was not an offer.
- Unilateral offers to the world can be offers, e.g. the reward advert in Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] 1 QB 256, where depositing money in a bank showed a serious intention to pay.

Acceptance
Acceptance must be an unqualified agreement to all the terms of the offer.
- A counter-offer rejects and destroys the original offer (Hyde v Wrench (1840)); a mere request for information does not (Stevenson, Jacques & Co v McLean (1880)).
- Battle of the forms: the courts usually apply the traditional offer and acceptance analysis, which tends to give victory to the "last shot" (Butler Machine Tool v Ex-Cell-O [1979] 1 WLR 401; Tekdata Interconnections v Amphenol [2009] EWCA Civ 1209).
- Silence is not normally acceptance (Felthouse v Bindley (1862)).
- In unilateral contracts, acceptance is by performance and need not be communicated in advance (Carlill).

Communication and the postal rule
Acceptance generally takes effect when communicated to the offeror. With instantaneous communication, it takes effect on receipt (Entores v Miles Far East [1955] 2 QB 327; Brinkibon v Stahag Stahl [1983] 2 AC 34). Where post is a reasonable means of acceptance, acceptance is complete on posting (Adams v Lindsell (1818)), even if the letter is lost (Household Fire Insurance v Grant (1879)). The offeror can exclude the rule, for example by requiring "notice in writing" (Holwell Securities v Hughes [1974] 1 WLR 155).

Termination of offers
- Revocation is possible at any time before acceptance, even if the offeror promised to keep the offer open (unless the offeree gave consideration for that promise).
- Revocation must be communicated, and the postal rule does not apply to it (Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880)). It may be communicated by a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds (1876)).
- For unilateral offers, the offeror cannot revoke once the offeree has started performing (Errington v Errington [1952] 1 KB 290).
- Offers also end on rejection, lapse of time or failure of a condition.

Certainty
The courts try to uphold bargains, especially where the parties have acted on them, but an agreement may be too vague or incomplete.
- Scammell v Ouston [1941] AC 251: "on hire-purchase terms" too vague.
- Hillas v Arcos (1932): an option was sufficiently certain given the parties' previous dealings.
- May and Butcher v R [1934] 2 KB 17n: price left to be agreed, so no contract.
- Walford v Miles [1992] 2 AC 128: a bare agreement to negotiate is unenforceable.
- RTS Flexible Systems v Molkerei Alois Müller [2010] UKSC 14: a contract can be found from conduct even where the parties said they would sign a formal document.

Exam tips: In problem questions, work through the timeline step by step: classify each communication (offer, invitation to treat, counter-offer, request for information, revocation), then decide when each took effect.

English law generally enforces only bargains, not bare promises (unless made by deed). Consideration is the element of exchange.

What counts as consideration
- Classic definition: some right, interest, profit or benefit to one party, or some forbearance, detriment, loss or responsibility suffered by the other (Currie v Misa (1875)).
- Lord Dunedin in Dunlop v Selfridge [1915] AC 847 adopted the idea of consideration as the "price" for which the promise is bought.
- Consideration must be sufficient but need not be adequate: Thomas v Thomas (1842) (£1 a year rent); Chappell v Nestlé [1960] AC 87 (chocolate wrappers).
- It must move from the promisee, although not necessarily to the promisor.

Past consideration
Something already done before the promise is not good consideration (Re McArdle [1951] Ch 669). An exception applies where the act was done at the promisor's request, both parties understood it would be paid for, and payment would have been legally enforceable had it been promised in advance (Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614, building on Lampleigh v Brathwait (1615)).

Performing an existing duty
- Public duty: doing only what the law already requires is not consideration (Collins v Godefroy (1831)); exceeding it may be.
- Duty owed to the promisor: Stilk v Myrick (1809) held that sailors who simply did their existing job could not enforce a promise of extra pay; compare Hartley v Ponsonby (1857), where so many crew had deserted that those remaining were doing more than their contract required.
- Williams v Roffey Bros [1991] 1 QB 1: a promise to pay more for the same work can be enforced where the promisor obtains a practical benefit (such as avoiding a penalty clause or the trouble of finding a replacement) and there is no economic duress or fraud.
- Duty owed to a third party: performing it can be consideration for a promise from someone else.

Part payment of debts
Paying part of a debt does not discharge the whole (Pinnel's Case (1602); Foakes v Beer (1884) 9 App Cas 605). In Re Selectmove [1995] 1 WLR 474 the Court of Appeal refused to extend Williams v Roffey to part payment. In MWB Business Exchange Centres v Rock Advertising [2018] UKSC 24 the Supreme Court decided the case on its no-oral-modification clause and declined to resolve this tension. Paying something different (a different thing, at a different place or earlier at the creditor's request) can be good consideration.

Promissory estoppel
Where a party to an existing legal relationship clearly promises not to enforce its strict rights, and the other party relies on it, the promisor may be prevented from going back on the promise where it would be inequitable to do so (Hughes v Metropolitan Railway (1877); Central London Property Trust v High Trees House [1947] KB 130).
- It is a "shield not a sword": it cannot create a new cause of action (Combe v Combe [1951] 2 KB 215).
- It is usually suspensory; rights can often be revived on reasonable notice (Tool Metal Manufacturing v Tungsten Electric [1955] 1 WLR 761), although past instalments that were forgiven may be extinguished.
- The promisee must not have acted inequitably (D & C Builders v Rees [1966] 2 QB 617).

Intention to create legal relations
- Domestic and social agreements: presumption against intention (Balfour v Balfour [1919] 2 KB 571; Jones v Padavatton [1969] 1 WLR 328), rebuttable, e.g. separated spouses (Merritt v Merritt [1970] 1 WLR 1211).
- Commercial agreements: strong presumption in favour (Edwards v Skyways [1964] 1 WLR 349), rebutted by clear words such as an "honourable pledge" clause (Rose and Frank v JR Crompton [1925] AC 445).

Exam tips: In variation problems, always ask (1) is there consideration (Roffey practical benefit, or is it part payment under Foakes)? (2) if not, does promissory estoppel help, and only as a defence?

notes.h: Interpreting express terms and implying terms
notes.body:
Once a contract exists, disputes often turn on what its terms mean. The courts' approach is objective: what would the words mean to a reasonable person with the background knowledge reasonably available to the parties when they contracted?

Express terms: the modern approach
- Investors Compensation Scheme v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896: Lord Hoffmann set out a contextual approach. Meaning is what the document would convey to a reasonable person with all the background knowledge reasonably available to the parties (the "matrix of fact"). Words are not always given their dictionary meaning if the background shows something has gone wrong with the language.
- Exclusions: previous negotiations (Prenn v Simmonds [1971] 1 WLR 1381) and declarations of subjective intent are not admissible for interpretation. Chartbrook v Persimmon Homes [2009] UKHL 38 confirmed the exclusion of prior negotiations, but also held that where something has clearly gone wrong with the language and it is clear what a reasonable person would understand was meant, the court can read the words accordingly.
- Rainy Sky v Kookmin Bank [2011] UKSC 50: where there are two possible meanings, the court may prefer the one more consistent with business common sense.
- Arnold v Britton [2015] UKSC 36: Lord Neuberger stressed that the natural meaning of the words is very important, that commercial common sense should not be used to undervalue the language, and that the court should not rewrite a bad bargain. A service charge clause was enforced according to its words even though it produced very high charges.
- Wood v Capita Insurance Services [2017] UKSC 24: Lord Hodge said textualism and contextualism are not rival schools but tools used in an iterative process; how much weight each gets depends on the contract (for example, a sophisticated professionally drafted contract may be read more textually).

Rectification is a separate equitable remedy that corrects a written document that fails to record the parties' actual agreement; it should not be confused with interpretation.

Implied terms
1. Terms implied in fact: implied into a particular contract to give effect to the parties' presumed intention.
- The Moorcock (1889) 14 PD 64: business efficacy.
- Shirlaw v Southern Foundries [1939] 2 KB 206: the "officious bystander" test (so obvious it goes without saying).
- Marks and Spencer v BNP Paribas [2015] UKSC 72: the test is necessity, not reasonableness. A term is implied only if it is necessary for business efficacy or so obvious it goes without saying; it must be capable of clear expression and must not contradict an express term. Lord Neuberger cautioned that the Privy Council's approach in Attorney General of Belize v Belize Telecom [2009] UKPC 10 should not be read as relaxing these tests. No term was implied requiring the landlord to refund rent paid in advance for the period after a break clause was exercised.
2. Terms implied in law: implied into all contracts of a defined type as a matter of policy, e.g. Liverpool City Council v Irwin [1977] AC 239 (landlord's duty to take reasonable care to maintain common parts of a tower block). The test is wider necessity for that type of contract.
3. Terms implied by statute: e.g. Sale of Goods Act 1979 ss12–15 (title, description, satisfactory quality, sample) in business-to-business sales; Consumer Rights Act 2015 ss9–11 for consumer goods contracts.
4. Terms implied by custom or course of dealing.

Exam tips: For interpretation essays, frame the debate as contextualism (ICS, Rainy Sky) versus a renewed emphasis on the words (Arnold v Britton), reconciled in Wood v Capita. For implied terms, always state the M&S necessity test and say whether the term is implied in fact or in law.

notes.h: Exemption clauses, statutory control and penalties
notes.body:
Exemption (exclusion and limitation) clauses allow a party to avoid or cap liability. English law controls them in three stages: incorporation, construction and statutory regulation. Penalty clauses are a further area where the courts refuse to enforce terms.

1. Incorporation
- Signature: a party who signs is generally bound whether or not they read the document (L'Estrange v Graucob [1934] 2 KB 394), unless the effect was misrepresented (Curtis v Chemical Cleaning and Dyeing [1951] 1 KB 805).
- Notice: reasonable notice must be given before or at the time of contracting (Parker v South Eastern Railway (1877); Olley v Marlborough Court [1949] 1 KB 532, where a notice in the hotel bedroom came too late). The document must be one expected to contain terms (Chapelton v Barry UDC [1940] 1 KB 532).
- The more onerous or unusual the term, the more must be done to draw attention to it (J Spurling v Bradshaw [1956] 1 WLR 461, Denning LJ's "red hand"; Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking [1971] 2 QB 163; Interfoto v Stiletto [1989] QB 433).
- A consistent course of dealing can incorporate terms (compare McCutcheon v David MacBrayne [1964] 1 WLR 125, where dealings were inconsistent).

2. Construction
- Ambiguity is resolved against the party relying on the clause (contra proferentem), though modern courts apply this less aggressively between commercial parties.
- Excluding liability for negligence requires clear words (Canada Steamship Lines v The King [1952] AC 192).
- There is no rule of law that a "fundamental breach" automatically defeats an exemption clause; it is a question of construction (Photo Production v Securicor [1980] AC 827).

3. Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (business-to-business and some other non-consumer contracts)
- s2(1): liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence cannot be excluded or restricted.
- s2(2): other loss caused by negligence can be excluded only if the term is reasonable.
- s3: where one party deals on the other's written standard terms of business, exclusions of liability for breach are subject to reasonableness.
- s6: liability for breach of the implied term as to title (Sale of Goods Act 1979 s12) cannot be excluded; the terms in ss13–15 can be excluded only if reasonable.
- s11: the term must be fair and reasonable in light of circumstances known or contemplated when the contract was made; the burden is on the party relying on it; Schedule 2 gives guidelines (bargaining strength, inducements, knowledge of the term, etc.); strictly these apply to ss6–7, but courts treat them as relevant generally.
- Cases: George Mitchell v Finney Lock Seeds [1983] 2 AC 803 (limitation to the price of defective seed unreasonable); Smith v Eric S Bush [1990] 1 AC 831 (surveyor's disclaimer unreasonable); Watford Electronics v Sanderson [2001] EWCA Civ 317 (courts should be slow to interfere where commercial parties of equal strength negotiated).

4. Consumer Rights Act 2015, Part 2 (trader–consumer contracts)
- s62: an unfair term is not binding on the consumer. A term is unfair if, contrary to the requirement of good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations to the consumer's detriment.
- s64: terms on the main subject matter or price are not assessed for fairness if transparent and prominent.
- Schedule 2 contains an indicative "grey list" of terms that may be unfair.
- s65: liability for death or personal injury from negligence cannot be excluded; s31 prevents exclusion of the statutory rights for goods.

5. Penalties
- Cavendish Square Holding v Makdessi; ParkingEye v Beavis [2015] UKSC 67 replaced the older focus on whether a clause was a "genuine pre-estimate of loss" (Dunlop v New Garage [1915] AC 79).
- The test: is the clause a secondary obligation (triggered by breach) imposing a detriment on the contract-breaker out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party in performance of the primary obligation?
- The rule applies only to clauses triggered by breach. In Beavis, an £85 overstay charge was valid because the operator had a legitimate interest in managing parking space.

Exam tips: Use the three-stage structure in problem questions, and identify early whether the claimant is a consumer (CRA 2015) or a business (UCTA 1977).

Vitiating factors may make a contract void (no contract at all) or voidable (valid until rescinded).

Misrepresentation: the elements
An actionable misrepresentation is an unambiguous false statement of existing fact (or law) made by one party to the other, which induces the other to enter the contract.
- Opinion is not fact (Bisset v Wilkinson [1927] AC 177), unless the maker has superior knowledge implying facts that justify it (Smith v Land and House Property Corp (1884)).
- A statement of intention can be a misrepresentation if the maker did not hold that intention: "the state of a man's mind is as much a fact as the state of his digestion" (Bowen LJ, Edgington v Fitzmaurice (1885)).
- Silence is generally not misrepresentation, but half-truths can be (Dimmock v Hallett (1866)), and a statement that becomes false before the contract must be corrected (With v O'Flanagan [1936] Ch 575).
- Inducement: the statement must have been a cause of entering the contract. It is no defence that the claimant could have discovered the truth (Redgrave v Hurd (1881)), but there is no inducement if the claimant relied entirely on their own investigations (Attwood v Small (1838)).

Types and damages
- Fraudulent: made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly, careless whether true or false (Derry v Peek (1889) 14 App Cas 337). Damages in the tort of deceit cover all direct losses, foreseeable or not.
- Negligent: either under Hedley Byrne v Heller [1964] AC 465 or, more usefully, under Misrepresentation Act 1967 s2(1). Under s2(1) the representor is liable unless they prove they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe, the statement was true. Royscot Trust v Rogerson [1991] 2 QB 297 held that damages are measured as if for fraud, a much-criticised result.
- Innocent: no damages as of right, but the court may award damages in lieu of rescission under s2(2).

Rescission
All misrepresentations make the contract voidable. Rescission is barred by affirmation (Long v Lloyd [1958] 1 WLR 753), lapse of time (Leaf v International Galleries [1950] 2 KB 86), intervening third-party rights, or where restoring the parties to their original positions is impossible. Under s3 of the 1967 Act, a clause excluding liability for misrepresentation must satisfy the UCTA reasonableness test.

Mistake

Common mistake (both parties share the same mistake)
- Non-existence of the subject matter can make the contract void (Couturier v Hastie (1856)).
- Mistake as to quality only voids the contract if it makes the subject matter essentially and radically different from what was believed (Bell v Lever Brothers [1932] AC 161).
- Great Peace Shipping v Tsavliris Salvage [2002] EWCA Civ 1407: a contract is void only if the shared assumption was fundamental, neither party warranted it, the mistake was not the fault of either party, and performance in line with the assumption is impossible. The court also held there is no separate equitable doctrine allowing rescission for common mistake, departing from Solle v Butcher [1950] 1 KB 671.

Unilateral mistake as to terms
A contract is void where one party is mistaken about the terms and the other knows it (Hartog v Colin and Shields [1939] 3 All ER 566). A mistake only about quality is not enough (Smith v Hughes (1871)).

Mistaken identity
- Face to face: a strong presumption that the seller intends to deal with the person in front of them, so the contract is only voidable for fraud (Phillips v Brooks [1919] 2 KB 243; Lewis v Averay [1972] 1 QB 198; contrast Ingram v Little [1961] 1 QB 31).
- In writing: the contract is with the person identified in the document, so a rogue posing as a named person makes no contract (Cundy v Lindsay (1878); Shogun Finance v Hudson [2003] UKHL 62, by a 3–2 majority).
- The distinction matters because an innocent third-party buyer gets good title only if the contract is voidable, not void.

Exam tips: For misrepresentation, always work through: statement of fact? inducement? which type? remedy and bars? For mistaken identity, the key issue is usually whether an innocent third party gets title.

notes.h: Duress, undue influence and unconscionable bargains
notes.body:
These doctrines deal with improper pressure or exploitation in the making of a contract. All make the contract voidable, so rescission is available subject to the usual bars.

Duress
Duress requires (1) illegitimate pressure that (2) caused the victim to enter the contract.
- Duress to the person: threats of violence. In Barton v Armstrong [1976] AC 104 (PC) the threat need only have been one reason for entering the contract, and the burden was on the threatener to show it contributed nothing.
- Duress of goods: threats to seize or damage property.
- Economic duress: recognised in Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614 and The Universe Sentinel [1983] 1 AC 366. The pressure must be illegitimate and a significant cause of the contract. Ordinary commercial pressure is not enough.
- Atlas Express v Kafco [1989] QB 833: a carrier threatened not to deliver unless paid more, knowing the small customer depended on meeting its supply contract with a major retailer; the agreement to pay more was voidable.
- DSND Subsea v Petroleum Geo-Services [2000] BLR 530 (Dyson J) gives a useful summary of factors: whether there was an actual or threatened breach, whether the threatening party acted in good faith, whether the victim had a realistic practical alternative, whether the victim protested, and whether it affirmed the contract.
- Threatening to break a contract is the usual illegitimate act. Threatening a lawful act is rarely duress: CTN Cash and Carry v Gallaher [1994] 4 All ER 714. In Times Travel v Pakistan International Airlines [2021] UKSC 40 the Supreme Court confirmed lawful act duress is very narrow, limited to morally reprehensible conduct such as exploiting knowledge of criminal activity, or using illegitimate means to manufacture a claim and then demanding payment in bad faith, and rejected the claim.
- Affirmation: delay in protesting can amount to affirmation (North Ocean Shipping v Hyundai (The Atlantic Baron) [1979] QB 705).

Undue influence
The leading case is Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2001] UKHL 44.
- Actual undue influence: the claimant proves that improper influence was exercised (for example, coercion or abuse of trust).
- Presumed (evidential) undue influence: the claimant proves (a) a relationship of trust and confidence and (b) a transaction that calls for explanation. The burden then shifts to the other party to rebut, often by showing independent advice was taken.
- Some relationships are treated as automatically involving trust and confidence (e.g. solicitor and client, doctor and patient, trustee and beneficiary, religious adviser and follower). Husband and wife is not one of them, so trust must be proved on the facts.
- Allcard v Skinner (1887) 36 Ch D 145: a nun's gifts to her order were affected by undue influence, though her claim was barred by delay.

Third parties and banks
Most cases involve a wife guaranteeing her husband's business debts to a bank.
- Barclays Bank v O'Brien [1994] 1 AC 180: the bank is "put on inquiry" when a wife stands surety for her husband's debts.
- CIBC Mortgages v Pitt [1994] 1 AC 200: no inquiry where a loan is made to both spouses jointly for their apparent joint benefit.
- Etridge: a bank is put on inquiry whenever the relationship between surety and debtor is non-commercial. It must then take reasonable steps, essentially ensuring the surety has received independent advice from a solicitor who explains the transaction. If it does so, the bank is protected even if undue influence occurred.

Unconscionable bargains
Equity may set aside a transaction where one party is at a serious disadvantage (for example poverty, ignorance or lack of advice) and the other exploits it in a morally culpable way, producing an oppressive bargain: Fry v Lane (1888); Alec Lobb Garages v Total Oil [1985] 1 WLR 173; Boustany v Pigott (1995) (PC). Inequality of bargaining power alone is not enough; English law has not adopted Lord Denning's general principle from Lloyds Bank v Bundy [1975] QB 326.

Exam tips: In surety problems, deal first with the wrongdoer (actual or presumed undue influence, or misrepresentation), then with whether the bank was put on inquiry and took the Etridge steps.

Frustration discharges a contract automatically when, without the fault of either party, a supervening event makes performance impossible, illegal or radically different from what was undertaken.

From absolute contracts to frustration
Originally contractual duties were absolute (Paradine v Jane (1647)). Taylor v Caldwell (1863) 3 B & S 826 introduced frustration: a music hall hired for concerts burned down before the dates, and both parties were excused. The court reasoned via an implied condition that the hall would continue to exist.

The modern test
Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC [1956] AC 696 rejected the implied term theory. Lord Radcliffe held frustration occurs where, without default of either party, a contractual obligation has become incapable of being performed because the circumstances would make it a thing radically different from that which was undertaken. Mere hardship, inconvenience or expense is not enough: in Davis a labour shortage that made the building project take much longer and cost more did not frustrate the contract. The Sea Angel [2007] EWCA Civ 547 adopted a "multi-factorial" approach looking at the terms, context, parties' knowledge and expectations, and the nature of the event.

Categories
- Destruction of subject matter: Taylor v Caldwell.
- Death or incapacity in personal service contracts.
- Frustration of common purpose: Krell v Henry [1903] 2 KB 740 (rooms hired to view coronation processions that were cancelled; frustrated) contrasted with Herne Bay Steam Boat v Hutton [1903] 2 KB 683 (boat hired to see a naval review and cruise round the fleet; not frustrated because the fleet could still be seen).
- Supervening illegality: e.g. trading with a country that becomes an enemy.
- Delay: very long delays can frustrate, but the Suez Canal closure in Tsakiroglou v Noblee Thorl [1962] AC 93 did not frustrate a sale requiring shipment, because the longer route round the Cape remained possible.
- Leases can in principle be frustrated (National Carriers v Panalpina [1981] AC 675), though rarely. In Canary Wharf (BP4) v European Medicines Agency [2019] EWHC 335 (Ch), Brexit did not frustrate the EMA's lease.

Limits
- Self-induced frustration does not count: Maritime National Fish v Ocean Trawlers [1935] AC 524 (PC); The Super Servant Two [1990] 1 Lloyd's Rep 1 (the party chose how to allocate its remaining vessel).
- Foreseen risks or events provided for in the contract (for example a force majeure clause) generally exclude frustration.
- Change in market conditions or the contract becoming unprofitable is not frustration.

Effects at common law
Frustration ends the contract automatically from the time of the event; it is not void from the start. Chandler v Webster [1904] 1 KB 493 left losses where they fell. Fibrosa v Fairbairn Lawson Combe Barbour [1943] AC 32 allowed recovery of money paid where there was a total failure of consideration, but this still left gaps.

Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943
- s1(2): money paid before frustration is recoverable, and money payable ceases to be payable. The court may allow the payee to keep or recover a sum for expenses incurred, up to the amount paid or payable before frustration.
- s1(3): where one party has obtained a valuable benefit (other than money) before frustration, the other may recover a just sum not exceeding the value of that benefit (BP Exploration v Hunt (No 2) [1979] 1 WLR 783, Robert Goff J).
- Gamerco v ICM/Fair Warning [1995] 1 WLR 1226: the court has a broad discretion over expenses and may allow nothing.
- s2(3): the parties may contract out. s2(5): certain contracts are excluded, including voyage charterparties (time and demise charterparties are covered), other contracts for the carriage of goods by sea, insurance and some sales of specific goods that perish.

Exam tips: In problems, first check whether the contract allocates the risk (force majeure clause), then apply Davis v Fareham, then check for self-induced frustration, and finally work through the 1943 Act for the financial consequences.

A breach occurs when a party, without lawful excuse, fails to perform a contractual obligation when due, performs defectively, or indicates that it will not perform. Liability for breach is generally strict: fault is irrelevant unless the term itself only requires reasonable care.

Not every breach allows termination
The innocent party can always claim damages, but may only terminate (bring future performance to an end) for a repudiatory breach. Whether a breach is repudiatory depends on the classification of the term.

Conditions, warranties and innominate terms
- Condition: an important term whose breach allows termination, however small the consequences (Poussard v Spiers (1876), a singer missing the opening performances). Terms can be conditions by statute (e.g. Sale of Goods Act 1979 ss12–15), by express designation, or by judicial classification. Time clauses in mercantile contracts are often conditions (Bunge v Tradax [1981] 1 WLR 711; The Mihalis Angelos [1971] 1 QB 164).
- Warranty: a less important term; breach gives damages only (Bettini v Gye (1876), a singer missing some rehearsals).
- Innominate (intermediate) term: the remedy depends on the seriousness of the breach. Hongkong Fir Shipping v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha [1962] 2 QB 26: seaworthiness was innominate; delays caused by an incompetent engine-room crew did not deprive the charterers of substantially the whole benefit of the two-year charter, so they could not terminate. See also The Hansa Nord [1976] QB 44.
- Calling a term a "condition" is not conclusive: Schuler v Wickman Machine Tool Sales [1974] AC 235, where a clause requiring weekly visits to customers was not a condition in the technical sense.
- The trade-off is certainty (conditions) versus flexibility and avoiding opportunistic termination (innominate terms).

Repudiation and renunciation
A party may also repudiate by showing a clear intention not to perform, or to perform in a way substantially inconsistent with its obligations. A party who in good faith takes a mistaken view of the contract does not necessarily repudiate (Woodar Investment v Wimpey [1980] 1 WLR 277).

Anticipatory breach
If a party repudiates before performance is due, the innocent party may sue at once (Hochster v De la Tour (1853) 2 E & B 678) or wait until performance is due.

The innocent party's election
- Terminate: the termination must be clearly communicated, though conduct (even not performing) can suffice (Vitol v Norelf (The Santa Clara) [1996] AC 800). Termination operates only for the future; it is not rescission from the start (Johnson v Agnew [1980] AC 367). Primary obligations to perform are replaced by a secondary obligation to pay damages (Photo Production v Securicor [1980] AC 827). Clauses such as arbitration and exemption clauses survive.
- Affirm: the contract stays alive for both parties, so the innocent party bears the risk of later events (Avery v Bowden (1855), where later war frustrated the contract) and remains bound by its own obligations (The Simona [1989] AC 788).
- White and Carter v McGregor [1962] AC 413: an innocent party who can perform without the other's cooperation may affirm, perform and claim the price, unless it has no legitimate interest in doing so rather than claiming damages (Lord Reid). The Alaskan Trader [1984] 1 All ER 129 applied the legitimate interest limit.

Entire obligations
Where payment is due only on complete performance, partial performance earns nothing (Cutter v Powell (1795); Sumpter v Hedges [1898] 1 QB 673). The doctrine of substantial performance softens this: where the work is substantially done, the price is payable less the cost of putting defects right (Hoenig v Isaacs [1952] 2 All ER 176; contrast Bolton v Mahadeva [1972] 1 WLR 1009).

Exam tips: In problems, classify each term, decide whether the breach is repudiatory, and then consider whether the innocent party has terminated or affirmed, including White and Carter if it wants to keep performing.

The default remedy for breach of contract is damages. Specific remedies and gain-based awards are exceptional.

Expectation damages
The aim is to put the claimant, so far as money can, in the position it would have been in had the contract been performed (Robinson v Harman (1848), Parke B).
- Difference in value vs cost of cure: Ruxley Electronics v Forsyth [1996] AC 344. A swimming pool was built shallower than agreed, which did not reduce its value. Rebuilding (over £20,000) was out of all proportion to the benefit, so the House of Lords upheld £2,500 for loss of amenity instead. Cost of cure is recoverable where reasonable and the claimant intends to carry out the work (Radford v De Froberville [1977] 1 WLR 1262).
- Reliance damages: wasted expenditure, including pre-contract expenditure in the parties' contemplation (Anglia Television v Reed [1972] 1 QB 60). The claimant cannot use reliance damages to escape a bad bargain (C & P Haulage v Middleton [1983] 1 WLR 1461).

Non-pecuniary loss
Generally not recoverable for disappointment or injured feelings (Addis v Gramophone [1909] AC 488). Exceptions: where a major or important object of the contract is to provide pleasure, relaxation or peace of mind (Jarvis v Swans Tours [1973] QB 233; Farley v Skinner [2001] UKHL 49), and for physical inconvenience and discomfort (Watts v Morrow [1991] 1 WLR 1421).

Limits on damages
1. Remoteness
- Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341: recoverable losses are those arising naturally in the usual course of things (first limb), or those that may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting as the probable result of breach (second limb, which depends on special knowledge).
- Victoria Laundry v Newman Industries [1949] 2 KB 528: late delivery of a boiler; normal lost profits recoverable but not the especially lucrative dyeing contracts, of which the defendants did not know.
- The Heron II [1969] 1 AC 350: the contract test is stricter than in tort, requiring the loss to be "not unlikely" or a "serious possibility".
- H Parsons (Livestock) v Uttley Ingham [1978] QB 791: if the type of loss is within contemplation, its extent need not be.
- Transfield Shipping v Mercator Shipping (The Achilleas) [2008] UKHL 48: Lords Hoffmann and Hope also asked whether the defendant had assumed responsibility for the type of loss; the owners could not recover the loss of a lucrative follow-on charter.
2. Causation: the breach must be an effective cause of the loss.
3. Mitigation: the claimant cannot recover loss it could reasonably have avoided (British Westinghouse v Underground Electric Railways [1912] AC 673; Payzu v Saunders [1919] 2 KB 581).

Agreed sums
A claim for the price or another agreed sum is a debt claim, not damages, so remoteness and mitigation do not apply (see White and Carter v McGregor [1962]).

Specific performance and injunctions
These are equitable and discretionary, available only where damages are inadequate.
- Land and unique goods are typical cases; Beswick v Beswick [1968] AC 58 ordered payment to a widow where damages would have been nominal.
- Courts will not usually order continuous activity requiring supervision: Co-operative Insurance v Argyll Stores [1998] AC 1 (no order to keep a supermarket open).
- Specific performance of personal service contracts is not ordered, but a negative injunction may restrain working for others (Lumley v Wagner (1852); Warner Bros v Nelson [1937] 1 KB 209).

Gain-based remedies
- Attorney-General v Blake [2001] 1 AC 268: an account of profits is available only in exceptional cases where normal remedies are inadequate and the claimant has a legitimate interest in depriving the defendant of profit.
- Negotiating damages (Wrotham Park Estate v Parkside Homes [1974] 1 WLR 798): Morris-Garner v One Step (Support) [2018] UKSC 20 held these are available where the breached right is itself an asset with economic value, such as a restrictive covenant over land, and not merely because ordinary damages are hard to quantify.

Exam tips: Structure answers as: measure (expectation, cost of cure or reliance) → heads of loss → remoteness → causation → mitigation → any alternative remedies.

cards.b: A statement inviting others to make offers, not itself an offer, e.g. goods on display (Boots [1953]; Fisher v Bell [1961]) or most adverts for sale (Partridge v Crittenden [1968]).

cards.f: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893]
cards.b: An advert promising £100 to anyone who used the smoke ball and caught flu was a unilateral offer to the world, accepted by performing the conditions; no prior notice of acceptance needed.
A counter-offer rejects the original offer, which cannot later be accepted.

Where post is a reasonable means of acceptance, acceptance takes effect on posting (Adams v Lindsell (1818)), even if lost (Household Fire v Grant (1879)). Excluded by express terms (Holwell v Hughes [1974]).
Acceptance by instantaneous means (telex, phone) takes effect when received by the offeror: Entores v Miles Far East [1955]; Brinkibon v Stahag Stahl [1983].
Revocation of an offer must be communicated to be effective; the postal rule does not apply to revocation.
Usually resolved by traditional offer and acceptance, so the last set of terms sent and accepted by conduct tends to win (Butler v Ex-Cell-O [1979]; Tekdata v Amphenol [2009]).
The House of Lords held that a bare agreement to negotiate (in good faith) is too uncertain to be enforced.
Consideration is some right, interest, profit or benefit to one party, or some forbearance, detriment, loss or responsibility given, suffered or undertaken by the other.
Consideration must have some value in the eyes of the law but the court will not assess whether it is a fair price: Thomas v Thomas (1842); Chappell v Nestlé [1960].
Past consideration is no consideration: a promise to pay for home improvements already completed was unenforceable.

cards.f: Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] past consideration test
cards.b: An earlier act is good consideration if done at the promisor's request, both understood it was to be paid for, and payment would have been enforceable if promised in advance.
A promise to pay more for existing contractual performance is enforceable if the promisor gains a practical benefit and there is no economic duress or fraud.
The House of Lords held that part payment of a debt is not consideration for a promise to forgo the balance (following Pinnel's Case).
Promissory estoppel is a shield, not a sword: it cannot be used to found a cause of action where there is no consideration.

cards.f: Presumptions on intention to create legal relations
cards.b: Domestic/social agreements: presumed not intended to be binding (Balfour v Balfour). Commercial agreements: presumed binding (Edwards v Skyways). Both rebuttable.
Lord Hoffmann: a contract means what it would convey to a reasonable person having all the background knowledge reasonably available to the parties at the time of contracting.
Evidence of pre-contractual negotiations is generally inadmissible to interpret a contract (Prenn v Simmonds [1971]; confirmed in Chartbrook v Persimmon [2009]).
Where a term has two possible meanings, the court is entitled to prefer the one most consistent with business common sense.
UKSC: natural meaning of the words is central; commercial common sense cannot be used to rewrite clear language to save a party from a bad bargain.
UKSC: textualism and contextualism are complementary tools, used iteratively; their relative weight depends on the nature and drafting of the contract.

cards.f: M&S v BNP Paribas [2015]: implication in fact
cards.b: A term is implied only if necessary for business efficacy or so obvious it goes without saying; reasonableness is not enough; it must not contradict express terms.
Example of a term implied in law: the landlord of a tower block must take reasonable care to maintain the common parts.
An exemption notice in a hotel bedroom was not incorporated because the contract had been made at reception before the guest could see it.
A particularly onerous or unusual term must be fairly and reasonably brought to the other party's attention to be incorporated; a heavy holding fee for late return was not.
No rule of law that fundamental breach destroys an exemption clause; it is a matter of construing the clause. The clause protected Securicor although its guard started a fire.
A person cannot by any contract term or notice exclude or restrict liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence.
The term must be fair and reasonable having regard to circumstances known or reasonably contemplated when the contract was made; the party relying on the term bears the burden.
A term is unfair if, contrary to good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations to the consumer's detriment. Unfair terms do not bind the consumer.
Terms setting the main subject matter or the price cannot be assessed for fairness on that basis if they are transparent and prominent.
A secondary obligation triggered by breach is penal if it imposes a detriment out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance of the primary obligation.
An unambiguous false statement of existing fact or law, made by one contracting party to the other, which induces the other to enter the contract.
A false statement of present intention is a misrepresentation of fact: 'the state of a man's mind is as much a fact as the state of his digestion' (Bowen LJ).
A false statement made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly, careless whether it is true or false.
Representor liable in damages for a misrepresentation unless they prove they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe, the facts were true. Royscot v Rogerson: fraud measure of damages.
Affirmation, lapse of time, intervening third-party rights, and impossibility of restoring the parties to their pre-contract positions.

cards.f: Great Peace Shipping [2002] common mistake test
cards.b: Void only if: shared fundamental assumption; no warranty by either party; not the fault of either; performance as assumed impossible. No equitable rescission for common mistake.
HL (3–2): a written hire-purchase agreement was with the person named in it, so the rogue had no contract or title and the innocent buyer did not acquire the car.
Face-to-face dealing: presumption that the seller intends to deal with the person present, so mistaken identity makes the contract voidable, not void.
Illegitimate pressure (usually a threatened breach of contract) that was a significant cause of the victim entering the contract, often judged by lack of a practical alternative.
A carrier's threat not to deliver unless paid more, exploiting the customer's dependence on a retail contract, was economic duress; the promise to pay more was voidable.
UKSC: lawful act duress exists but is very narrow, requiring morally reprehensible or bad-faith conduct; hard commercial bargaining with a dominant position is not enough.
Claimant shows a relationship of trust and confidence plus a transaction that calls for explanation; the burden then shifts to the defendant to rebut the inference.

cards.f: When is a bank 'put on inquiry' (Etridge)?
cards.b: Whenever a person stands surety for the debts of another with whom they have a non-commercial relationship, e.g. a wife guaranteeing her husband's business debts.
The bank should ensure the surety receives independent advice from a solicitor who explains the nature and risks of the transaction, and obtain confirmation of this.
Duress to the person: the threat need only be one reason for entering the contract; the threatener must show it contributed nothing.
A music hall hired for concerts was destroyed by fire without fault; the contract was discharged because performance depended on the hall continuing to exist.

cards.f: Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC [1956] test
cards.b: Frustration occurs where, without default of either party, performance would be radically different from that undertaken. Increased cost or delay alone is not enough.

cards.f: Krell v Henry vs Herne Bay v Hutton (1903)
cards.b: Krell: rooms to watch coronation processions; cancellation frustrated the whole purpose. Herne Bay: boat hire to see the naval review still had value (cruise round the fleet), so no frustration.
The closure of the Suez Canal did not frustrate a contract to ship groundnuts; the longer route via the Cape made performance more costly, not radically different.
A party cannot rely on an event caused by its own choice or default: Maritime National Fish [1935] (allocation of licences); The Super Servant Two [1990].
Money paid before frustration is recoverable; money payable ceases to be payable; the court may allow the payee to retain or recover expenses up to the sum paid or payable.
A party who conferred a valuable non-money benefit before frustration may recover a just sum not exceeding that benefit's value (BP v Hunt (No 2)).
A term so important that any breach entitles the innocent party to terminate and claim damages, regardless of the actual consequences (e.g. Poussard v Spiers (1876)).
A less important term; breach gives a right to damages only, not termination (e.g. Bettini v Gye (1876)).
For innominate terms, termination is only allowed if the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit it was intended to obtain from the contract.
Labelling a term a 'condition' is not conclusive; the court asks whether the parties really intended any breach, however trivial, to allow termination.
Anticipatory breach: where a party renounces before performance is due, the innocent party may sue immediately without waiting for the performance date.
Innocent party may affirm, perform and claim the price if it needs no cooperation, unless it has no legitimate interest in performing rather than claiming damages.
Operates prospectively, not from the start (Johnson v Agnew); primary obligations are replaced by a secondary duty to pay damages (Photo Production); exemption and dispute clauses survive.
Where an entire obligation is substantially performed, the price is payable less the cost of remedying defects: Hoenig v Isaacs [1952]; contrast Bolton v Mahadeva [1972].
Expectation principle: damages should put the claimant, so far as money can, in the position it would have been in had the contract been performed.
Cost of cure refused as unreasonable where out of all proportion to the benefit; the claimant got £2,500 for loss of amenity for a shallower-than-agreed pool.
Recoverable: (1) losses arising naturally in the usual course of things; (2) losses within both parties' reasonable contemplation at contracting as the probable result of breach.
Contract remoteness requires the loss to have been contemplated as 'not unlikely' or a 'serious possibility' at the time of contracting; stricter than the tort test.
HL: the charterer was not liable for the owners' lost follow-on fixture; Lords Hoffmann and Hope reasoned it had not assumed responsibility for that type of loss.
The claimant cannot recover losses it could reasonably have avoided; reasonable mitigation costs are recoverable (British Westinghouse [1912]; Payzu v Saunders [1919]).
HL refused specific performance of a covenant to keep a supermarket open: it would require constant supervision and could cause wasteful losses.
UKSC: negotiating (Wrotham Park) damages are available where the right breached is an asset with economic value, not just because loss is hard to measure.

questions.q: On Monday A posts a letter offering to sell his car to B for £5,000. On Wednesday A posts a letter revoking the offer. B receives the offer on Wednesday and posts an acceptance at once. B receives the revocation on Friday. Applying the classic rules, is there a contract?
options: No, because the revocation was posted before B posted the acceptance
Yes, because the acceptance took effect on posting, before the revocation was received
No, because acceptance by post is only effective on receipt
Yes, but only if A received the acceptance before Friday
questions.why: Revocation must be communicated, so it only takes effect when B receives it on Friday (Byrne v Van Tienhoven). B's acceptance took effect on posting on Wednesday under the postal rule (Adams v Lindsell), so a contract was formed then. Saying the earlier-posted revocation wins wrongly applies the postal rule to revocation; saying acceptance by post needs receipt states the instantaneous-communication rule instead; and whether A received the acceptance before Friday is irrelevant, because receipt is not required under the postal rule.

questions.q: Which case held that goods displayed on shelves in a self-service shop are an invitation to treat, so the customer makes the offer at the cash desk?
options: Fisher v Bell [1961]
Partridge v Crittenden [1968]
Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists [1953]
Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893]
questions.why: Boots concerned self-service shelves. Fisher v Bell was about a flick knife in a shop window; Partridge v Crittenden about a newspaper advert for birds; Carlill found an advert to be a unilateral offer.

questions.q: Explain how English law treats the 'battle of the forms', with reference to case law.
markScheme: Identifies the problem: parties exchange standard terms that conflict, so it is unclear whether and on whose terms a contract exists
Explains the traditional offer/counter-offer analysis and that each new form is a counter-offer (Hyde v Wrench)
Uses Butler Machine Tool v Ex-Cell-O [1979]: the buyer's terms prevailed as the seller returned the acknowledgment slip
Notes Lord Denning's broader 'whole documents' approach was not adopted by the majority
Cites Tekdata v Amphenol [2009]: traditional analysis is the starting point, departed from only where the parties' conduct clearly shows a different intention
questions.modelAnswer: When businesses exchange their own standard forms, each set of terms usually conflicts with the last, so the question is whether a contract exists and on whose terms. English law generally applies the traditional offer and acceptance model. Each form that introduces different terms is a counter-offer, which destroys the previous offer (Hyde v Wrench). The contract is concluded when one party accepts the latest counter-offer, either expressly or by conduct such as delivering or accepting the goods. This often means the 'last shot' wins. In Butler Machine Tool v Ex-Cell-O [1979], the seller's quotation contained a price variation clause, but the buyer ordered on its own terms with a tear-off acknowledgment, which the seller signed and returned. The Court of Appeal held the contract was on the buyer's terms. Lord Denning suggested looking at the documents as a whole, but the other judges used the orthodox analysis. In Tekdata v Amphenol [2009], the Court of Appeal confirmed that the traditional approach is the starting point and will only be displaced where the documents or conduct clearly show the parties intended something else, which gives commercial certainty.

questions.q: B owes C £10,000. C agrees to accept £6,000 in full settlement, and B pays. C now sues for £4,000. Which statement best reflects the current law?
options: C cannot recover because B provided a practical benefit under Williams v Roffey
C can in principle recover because part payment is not consideration (Foakes v Beer), subject to any promissory estoppel argument
C cannot recover because the Supreme Court in MWB v Rock overruled Foakes v Beer
C can recover only if the agreement was not in writing
questions.why: Foakes v Beer remains binding: part payment is not good consideration, and Re Selectmove refused to apply Roffey to part payment of debts. MWB v Rock left the point open rather than overruling Foakes. Writing is irrelevant to consideration. B may try promissory estoppel, but must show it would be inequitable for C to go back on the promise (compare D & C Builders v Rees).

questions.q: Which case established a presumption that agreements between spouses living together are not intended to be legally binding?
options: Merritt v Merritt [1970]
Balfour v Balfour [1919]
Edwards v Skyways [1964]
Jones v Padavatton [1969]
questions.why: Balfour v Balfour concerned a husband's promise of a monthly allowance to his wife while they were living together. Merritt concerned separated spouses, where the presumption was rebutted; Edwards v Skyways concerns commercial agreements; Jones v Padavatton involved a mother and daughter.

questions.q: Explain the requirements of promissory estoppel and its main limits.
markScheme: Existing legal relationship between the parties (Hughes v Metropolitan Railway)
Clear and unequivocal promise or representation not to enforce strict legal rights
Reliance by the promisee on the promise (High Trees)
Inequitable for the promisor to go back on it; promisee must have acted equitably (D & C Builders v Rees)
Limits: shield not sword (Combe v Combe) and usually suspensory, revivable on reasonable notice (Tool Metal v Tungsten)
questions.modelAnswer: Promissory estoppel developed from Hughes v Metropolitan Railway (1877) and was revived by Denning J in Central London Property Trust v High Trees House [1947]. It requires an existing legal relationship, usually a contract, and a clear and unequivocal promise by one party that it will not enforce its strict legal rights. The promisee must have relied on that promise, typically by acting differently from how it otherwise would. Finally, it must be inequitable for the promisor to resile. The promisee must also have clean hands: in D & C Builders v Rees [1966] the debtor's wife exploited the builders' financial difficulty, so the defence failed. There are important limits. First, the doctrine operates as a shield, not a sword: in Combe v Combe [1951] a former wife could not sue on a promise of maintenance unsupported by consideration. Second, its effect is usually suspensory: the promisor can often reinstate its rights for the future by giving reasonable notice (Tool Metal Manufacturing v Tungsten Electric [1955]), although sums already forgone may be permanently lost.

questions.q: According to Marks and Spencer v BNP Paribas [2015], which statement about implying terms in fact is correct?
options: A term will be implied if it would be fair and reasonable
A term will be implied if necessary for business efficacy or so obvious it goes without saying
A term may be implied even if it contradicts an express term
Implication is simply part of the process of interpretation and needs no separate test
questions.why: The Supreme Court confirmed the strict business efficacy and obviousness tests. A term is not implied just because it would be fair and reasonable; an implied term cannot contradict an express one; and Lord Neuberger stressed that implication is a separate exercise with its own tests, rejecting a reading of Belize Telecom that treated it as just interpretation.

questions.q: In Chartbrook v Persimmon Homes [2009], the House of Lords:
options: abolished the rule excluding evidence of prior negotiations
kept the exclusionary rule but read the formula in the way the reasonable person would have understood it, given an obvious drafting error
held that the court may never depart from the literal meaning of words
ordered rectification because the parties' subjective intentions differed
questions.why: Lord Hoffmann declined to abolish the exclusion of prior negotiations, but held that where something had clearly gone wrong with the language and the intended meaning was clear, the clause could be construed accordingly. The decision rested on construction, not on abolishing the rule or on subjective intentions, and the idea that courts may never depart from literal meaning is contrary to the contextual approach.

questions.q: Distinguish between terms implied in fact and terms implied in law, giving an authority for each.
markScheme: Terms implied in fact give effect to the presumed intention of the parties in a particular contract
Test: necessity for business efficacy or obviousness (The Moorcock; Shirlaw; M&S v BNP Paribas)
Terms implied in law are default rules for all contracts of a particular type, based on policy
Test for implication in law is wider necessity for that kind of contract (Liverpool CC v Irwin)
Both are excluded by inconsistent express terms
questions.modelAnswer: Terms implied in fact are read into a particular contract because the court concludes the parties must have intended them. The court applies a strict test: the term must be necessary to give the contract business efficacy (The Moorcock (1889)) or so obvious that it goes without saying (Shirlaw v Southern Foundries [1939]). In Marks and Spencer v BNP Paribas [2015] the Supreme Court confirmed that reasonableness is not enough and declined to imply a term requiring rent to be refunded after a break clause was exercised. Terms implied in law are different: they are standard incidents attached to every contract of a particular kind, such as employment, landlord and tenant or sale, for reasons of policy. The test is whether the term is necessary for that type of contract, which is a broader question than in fact. In Liverpool City Council v Irwin [1977], the House of Lords implied into tenancies of a council tower block a duty on the landlord to take reasonable care to keep the common parts in repair. Either type can be excluded by a clear contrary express term.

questions.q: A business-to-business contract on the supplier's written standard terms excludes all liability for late delivery. Under UCTA 1977, the exclusion is:
options: automatically void
valid only if it satisfies the requirement of reasonableness
valid without restriction because both parties are businesses
subject to the CRA 2015 fairness test
questions.why: Under s3 UCTA, where one party deals on the other's written standard terms of business, terms excluding liability for breach are subject to the s11 reasonableness test. Only certain liabilities (e.g. death or personal injury from negligence, s2(1)) are automatically ineffective. The CRA 2015 applies to trader–consumer contracts, not business-to-business ones.

questions.q: In ParkingEye v Beavis [2015], the £85 charge for overstaying was upheld mainly because:
options: it was a genuine pre-estimate of the operator's loss
the penalty rule never applies to consumer contracts
the operator and landowner had a legitimate interest in efficient use of parking spaces, and the charge was not out of all proportion to it
Mr Beavis had signed a written contract
questions.why: The Supreme Court held the charge was not penal under the new legitimate interest test. It was clearly not a genuine pre-estimate of loss (the operator lost little from one overstay); the penalty rule can apply to consumer contracts; and the contract was made by parking under clear signage, not by signing anything.

questions.q: Explain the three-stage approach to exemption clauses, illustrating each stage with an authority.
markScheme: Incorporation: signature (L'Estrange v Graucob) or reasonable notice before contracting (Olley v Marlborough Court)
Onerous terms need greater notice (Interfoto; Spurling v Bradshaw)
Construction: contra proferentem and clear words needed to exclude negligence (Canada Steamship)
No doctrine of fundamental breach as a rule of law (Photo Production v Securicor)
Statutory control: UCTA 1977 (business contracts, reasonableness in s11) or CRA 2015 (consumer contracts, s62 fairness)
questions.modelAnswer: First, the clause must be incorporated into the contract. A signature normally binds (L'Estrange v Graucob [1934]); otherwise, reasonable notice must be given before or when the contract is made, so a notice seen only after contracting is ineffective (Olley v Marlborough Court [1949]). The more onerous the term, the greater the notice required (Spurling v Bradshaw [1956]; Interfoto v Stiletto [1989]). Second, the clause must cover the loss on its true construction. Ambiguities are read against the party relying on it, and clear words are needed to exclude liability for negligence (Canada Steamship Lines v The King [1952]). There is no rule that a serious breach automatically defeats the clause; in Photo Production v Securicor [1980] the House of Lords held it is purely a question of construction. Third, the clause must survive statutory control. In business contracts, UCTA 1977 makes some exclusions void (death or personal injury from negligence, s2(1)) and subjects others to the reasonableness test in s11. In consumer contracts, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 applies: s65 bars exclusion of negligence liability for death or personal injury and s62 renders unfair terms non-binding on the consumer.

questions.q: S, selling a hotel, says 'the hotel takes £200,000 a year'. That was true when said, but takings fall sharply before contracts are exchanged and S says nothing. B buys. What is the best analysis?
options: No misrepresentation, because the statement was true when made
Misrepresentation, because a statement that becomes false before the contract must be corrected (With v O'Flanagan)
No misrepresentation, because silence can never be a misrepresentation
Only a claim for breach of contract is possible
questions.why: With v O'Flanagan [1936] holds that a representation continues until the contract is made, so a change that makes it false must be disclosed. Saying it was true when made, or that silence can never be a misrepresentation, ignores this exception to the general rule that silence is not misrepresentation. Whether the statement was also a term is a separate question; misrepresentation remedies are available.

questions.q: Under Bell v Lever Brothers [1932], a common mistake as to the quality of the subject matter makes a contract void only if:
options: one party would not have entered the contract had they known the truth
it makes the subject matter essentially and radically different from what both parties believed
the mistaken party has suffered a financial loss
the other party knew of the mistake
questions.why: The House of Lords set a very high threshold: the mistake must make the thing essentially different from what it was believed to be. Bell itself failed this test. 'Would not have entered the contract had they known' describes inducement in misrepresentation; financial loss is irrelevant; and the other party knowing of the mistake describes unilateral mistake as to terms (Hartog v Colin and Shields).

questions.q: Explain the remedies available for negligent and innocent misrepresentation under the Misrepresentation Act 1967.
markScheme: All types of misrepresentation make the contract voidable; rescission available subject to bars
s2(1): damages unless representor proves reasonable grounds for belief; burden reversed
Royscot v Rogerson: s2(1) damages measured as in fraud (all direct loss)
s2(2): court may award damages in lieu of rescission for non-fraudulent misrepresentation
Innocent misrepresentation: no damages as of right; s3 subjects exclusion clauses to UCTA reasonableness
questions.modelAnswer: All misrepresentations make a contract voidable, so the representee may rescind unless barred by affirmation, lapse of time, third-party rights or impossibility of restitution. For damages, the most useful route for negligent misrepresentation is s2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act 1967. The representee need not prove fraud or a duty of care; the representor is liable unless they prove they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe up to the time of contracting, that the facts were true. This reversal of the burden makes s2(1) attractive compared with Hedley Byrne. In Royscot Trust v Rogerson [1991] the Court of Appeal held that s2(1) damages are measured as in fraud, so the claimant recovers all losses directly flowing from the misrepresentation, even if unforeseeable; this is widely criticised. Where the misrepresentation is wholly innocent, there is no right to damages, but under s2(2) the court may declare the contract subsisting and award damages in lieu of rescission if that would be equitable. Section 3 provides that a term excluding liability for misrepresentation is effective only if it satisfies the reasonableness test in UCTA.

questions.q: Which relationship is NOT treated as automatically involving trust and confidence for presumed undue influence?
options: Solicitor and client
Doctor and patient
Husband and wife
Trustee and beneficiary
questions.why: In Etridge the House of Lords confirmed that husband and wife is not in the automatic category; a wife must prove she placed trust and confidence in her husband in financial matters. The other three are recognised categories where trust and confidence is presumed irrebuttably.

questions.q: In CTN Cash and Carry v Gallaher [1994], the supplier's demand for payment backed by a threat to withdraw credit facilities was:
options: economic duress, because the threat was illegitimate
not duress, because the threatened act was lawful and the supplier believed in good faith the money was owed
undue influence, because the buyer depended on the supplier
void for mistake
questions.why: The Court of Appeal held there was no duress: withdrawing credit was lawful and the demand was made in a bona fide belief that payment was due. Lawful act duress is very narrow, as later confirmed in Times Travel v PIA. Undue influence and mistake are different doctrines and were not in issue.

questions.q: W signed a charge over the family home to guarantee her husband H's business overdraft with Bank X after H told her it was 'just a formality'. Bank X sent her no letter and she had no legal advice. Advise W.
markScheme: Identify possible wrong by H: misrepresentation and/or undue influence (actual or presumed under Etridge)
Presumed undue influence: W must prove trust and confidence in H on finances; guarantee of husband's debts calls for explanation
Bank put on inquiry: non-commercial surety relationship (O'Brien; Etridge)
Bank failed to take reasonable steps (no independent solicitor's advice or confirmation)
Conclusion: bank fixed with constructive notice, so W can likely have the charge set aside against the bank
questions.modelAnswer: W must first show a wrong by H. His statement that the charge was 'just a formality' is likely a misrepresentation of its effect. She may also argue undue influence. Husband and wife is not an automatic trust relationship, so she must prove she trusted H to manage financial matters; if so, a guarantee of his business debts with her home at stake is a transaction that calls for explanation, so the burden shifts to H to rebut the inference (Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2001]). Next, W needs to make the wrong bind Bank X. Under Barclays Bank v O'Brien [1994] and Etridge, a bank is put on inquiry whenever someone stands surety for the debts of another in a non-commercial relationship. This applies here, and the joint loan exception in CIBC v Pitt does not apply because the borrowing is for H's business. Once on inquiry, the bank must take reasonable steps, essentially making sure W gets independent advice from a solicitor and receiving confirmation of it. Bank X did none of this, so it has constructive notice of H's wrong. W can therefore probably have the charge set aside as against the bank, subject to bars such as affirmation.

questions.q: A builder's contract becomes 50% more expensive because of a sudden rise in material prices. Is the contract frustrated?
options: Yes, because performance has become much more onerous
No, because increased expense does not make performance radically different (Davis Contractors v Fareham)
Yes, but only under the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943
No, because frustration only applies where the subject matter is destroyed
questions.why: Davis v Fareham and Tsakiroglou show that greater cost or difficulty is not frustration. The 1943 Act deals only with the consequences of frustration, not whether it has occurred. Frustration is not limited to destruction of the subject matter: frustration of purpose, illegality and delay can also frustrate.

questions.q: Under s1(2) of the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943, a payee who has incurred expenses before frustration:
options: is always entitled to keep all advance payments
may be allowed by the court to keep or recover a sum for expenses, not exceeding the amount paid or payable before frustration
may recover all expenses regardless of whether anything was paid or payable
can never recover expenses
questions.why: The expenses proviso in s1(2) is discretionary and capped at sums paid or payable before the frustrating event. In Gamerco v ICM the judge used this discretion to allow nothing. There is no automatic right to keep all advance payments, no uncapped recovery of expenses, and it is wrong to say expenses can never be recovered.

questions.q: Explain why self-induced frustration does not discharge a contract, using case law.
markScheme: Frustration requires the event to occur without the fault or choice of the party relying on it
Maritime National Fish v Ocean Trawlers [1935]: company chose which trawlers to use its limited licences for
The Super Servant Two [1990]: choosing how to allocate the remaining vessel was the party's own election
Rationale: a party should not escape obligations by its own choice; risk allocation and fairness
Burden of proving default lies on the party alleging it (Joseph Constantine Steamship v Imperial Smelting [1942])
questions.modelAnswer: Frustration only operates where the supervening event happens without the default of either party; otherwise a party could escape a bad bargain by its own conduct. In Maritime National Fish v Ocean Trawlers [1935] the charterers of a trawler received only three fishing licences for the five vessels they operated and chose to allocate them to other ships. They could not claim the charter was frustrated, because the lack of a licence for that trawler resulted from their own choice. Similarly in The Super Servant Two [1990], a company that had two vessels capable of performing several contracts lost one, and chose to use the remaining vessel for other contracts. The Court of Appeal held the failure to perform was caused by its own election, not by the sinking. Where frustration is disputed, the party alleging that the frustrating event was self-induced must prove it (Joseph Constantine Steamship v Imperial Smelting [1942] AC 154).

questions.q: In Hongkong Fir Shipping v Kawasaki [1962], the charterers could NOT terminate because:
options: the seaworthiness obligation was a warranty
the seaworthiness obligation was a condition, but they had affirmed
it was an innominate term and the breach did not deprive them of substantially the whole benefit of the charter
the delay was caused by frustration
questions.why: The Court of Appeal held that seaworthiness was an innominate term, so the right to terminate depended on the seriousness of the consequences; the delays did not deprive the charterers of substantially the whole benefit. It was not classified as a condition or warranty, and frustration was not the basis of the decision.

questions.q: A advertises on B's billboards for three years; on the day the contract is signed, A cancels. B, who needs nothing from A to perform, displays the adverts and sues for the full price. Applying White and Carter v McGregor, B:
options: must accept the repudiation and can only claim damages
can recover the price unless it had no legitimate interest in performing rather than claiming damages
can recover nothing because it failed to mitigate
can recover the price only if A acted in bad faith
questions.why: In White and Carter the House of Lords allowed the innocent party to affirm, perform and recover the price, subject to Lord Reid's qualification that it may lose this right if it has no legitimate interest in performing. It need not accept the repudiation, mitigation does not apply to a claim for an agreed sum, and bad faith is not required.

questions.q: Explain the options open to an innocent party faced with an anticipatory repudiation.
markScheme: Definition: renunciation of the contract before performance is due
Option 1: accept the repudiation, terminate and sue immediately (Hochster v De la Tour)
Acceptance must be clear but may be by conduct (Vitol v Norelf)
Option 2: affirm and keep the contract alive for both sides; risk of supervening events (Avery v Bowden; The Simona)
If affirming and able to perform without cooperation, may claim price subject to legitimate interest (White and Carter)
questions.modelAnswer: An anticipatory repudiation occurs when a party, before performance is due, shows clearly that it will not perform or will not perform in a way that goes to the root of the contract. The innocent party has a choice. First, it can accept the repudiation, terminate, and sue straight away for damages, as in Hochster v De la Tour (1853), where a courier hired to start work in June could sue in May when his employer cancelled. Acceptance must be unequivocal but can be communicated by conduct, including simply not performing (Vitol v Norelf [1996]). Second, it can affirm and wait for the time for performance. The contract then stays alive for both parties: the innocent party must still perform its own obligations (The Simona [1989]) and takes the risk of later events, such as the frustrating war in Avery v Bowden (1855), which removed the claim. If the innocent party can perform without the other's cooperation, White and Carter v McGregor [1962] allows it to perform and claim the contract price, unless it had no legitimate interest in doing so.

questions.q: A laundry ordered a boiler that was delivered five months late. It could recover its ordinary lost profits but not the profits from unusually lucrative government dyeing contracts. Which case is this?
options: Hadley v Baxendale (1854)
Victoria Laundry v Newman Industries [1949]
The Heron II [1969]
H Parsons v Uttley Ingham [1978]
questions.why: These are the facts of Victoria Laundry. Hadley v Baxendale concerned a delayed crankshaft and a mill; The Heron II a delayed sugar cargo and a falling market; Parsons a defective hopper and dead pigs.

questions.q: Which statement about reliance damages is correct?
options: They can never include expenditure before the contract was made
They allow a claimant to recover wasted expenditure even if the contract would have made a loss anyway
They may include pre-contract expenditure in the parties' contemplation, but cannot put the claimant in a better position than performance would have
They are only available when expectation loss is easy to prove
questions.why: Anglia Television v Reed allowed pre-contract expenditure that was within the parties' contemplation, so it is wrong to say such expenditure is never included. C & P Haulage v Middleton shows reliance damages cannot be used to escape a bad bargain. Reliance damages are typically claimed when expectation loss is hard to prove, so 'only when expectation loss is easy to prove' is the opposite of the usual position.

questions.q: When will a court award specific performance rather than damages for breach of contract?
markScheme: Specific performance is equitable and discretionary; damages are the primary remedy
Available where damages are inadequate, e.g. land or unique goods; Beswick v Beswick (damages nominal)
Refused where constant supervision needed or for continuing activity (Co-op v Argyll)
Not ordered for personal service contracts; negative injunctions may be granted (Lumley v Wagner; Warner Bros v Nelson)
Other bars: hardship, delay, claimant's conduct ('clean hands')
questions.modelAnswer: Damages are the normal remedy, and specific performance is an equitable remedy granted at the court's discretion, mainly where damages would be inadequate. This is presumed for contracts for the sale of land, because each piece of land is treated as unique, and may apply to unique goods. In Beswick v Beswick [1968] specific performance was ordered requiring a nephew to pay an annuity to his uncle's widow, because damages to the estate would have been nominal. The court will usually refuse where an order would require constant supervision or continuing activity: in Co-operative Insurance v Argyll Stores [1998] the House of Lords would not order a supermarket to keep trading, partly because the tenant would be forced to run a loss-making business. Contracts for personal services are not specifically enforced, although a negative injunction may restrain working for a competitor where this does not in practice compel performance (Lumley v Wagner (1852); Warner Bros v Nelson [1937]). The remedy may also be refused for severe hardship, delay or the claimant's own unfair conduct.

questions.q: Problem question. Dina runs a small catering business. In March she negotiated to buy a commercial oven from Ovenco Ltd. Ovenco's salesperson told her, 'This model will cook 500 meals an hour; I'm sure you will double your output.' In fact the model can cook only 300 meals an hour, as the salesperson would have known had he checked the specification sheet in his folder. Dina signed Ovenco's order form, which stated on its reverse: 'Ovenco shall not be liable for any statement made by its staff, or for any loss of profit howsoever caused.' Dina did not read the reverse. The oven was delivered on 1 May, five weeks late, causing Dina to lose an ordinary catering job worth £4,000 profit and a one-off, exceptionally lucrative contract to cater a celebrity wedding worth £20,000 profit, which she had not mentioned to Ovenco. Advise Dina.
markScheme: Misrepresentation: '500 meals an hour' is a statement of fact (verifiable); 'double your output' is opinion/puffery (Bisset v Wilkinson); inducement (Redgrave v Hurd)
Classification: at least negligent; s2(1) Misrepresentation Act 1967 with reversed burden; Royscot fraud measure; rescission and its bars (affirmation, lapse of time)
Possibility the statement is also a term (breach of contract claim) and implied terms on description/quality where relevant
Exemption clause: incorporation by signature (L'Estrange v Graucob); construction (contra proferentem)
