Statutory control: Dina contracts as a business so UCTA 1977 not CRA 2015; s3 Misrepresentation Act 1967 and UCTA s11 reasonableness; s3 UCTA written standard terms; factors (bargaining power, insurance, Sch 2; George Mitchell; Watford Electronics)
Late delivery as breach; whether time was of the essence/termination not needed as Dina wants damages
Remoteness: £4,000 ordinary profit within Hadley limb 1/Victoria Laundry; £20,000 wedding profit not recoverable without special knowledge (limb 2)
Mitigation and a reasoned conclusion on likely recovery
questions.modelAnswer:
Misrepresentation. The salesperson's claim that the oven cooks 500 meals an hour is a verifiable statement of existing fact, not opinion. By contrast, 'I'm sure you will double your output' is a forecast and likely an opinion (Bisset v Wilkinson [1927]), although a seller with superior knowledge may imply facts supporting it (Smith v Land and House). The 500-meal statement probably induced Dina to buy; it is no defence that she could have checked (Redgrave v Hurd). Because the salesperson had the specification sheet and did not check it, he lacked reasonable grounds for belief, so Ovenco is liable under s2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act 1967 unless it can prove such grounds, which looks unlikely. Under Royscot v Rogerson damages follow the fraud measure, covering all losses flowing directly from entering the contract. Dina could also try to rescind, but she must act promptly: continued use after discovering the truth may amount to affirmation, and lapse of time may bar relief (Leaf v International Galleries). The statement may also have become a term, giving a parallel claim for breach.

The exemption clause. Dina signed the form, so the clause is incorporated even though she did not read it (L'Estrange v Graucob). On construction, the first limb clearly covers misrepresentation and the second covers loss of profit. Because Dina buys as a business, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 does not apply. Section 3 of the 1967 Act makes the exclusion of misrepresentation liability subject to the UCTA s11 reasonableness test, and because Dina appears to deal on Ovenco's written standard terms, s3 UCTA also applies the test to excluding liability for breach. Ovenco must prove the clause was reasonable. Relevant factors are the parties' relative bargaining power (Dina is a small business), whether she could have bought elsewhere without such a term, whether Ovenco could insure, and how wide the clause is. A blanket exclusion of all liability for staff statements, together with all loss of profit 'howsoever caused', is likely to be unreasonable (compare George Mitchell v Finney Lock Seeds), although courts are reluctant to interfere between commercial parties of equal strength (Watford Electronics). On these facts it is probably unreasonable.

Late delivery. Delivering five weeks late is a breach. Dina wants damages, so termination need not be considered. Under Hadley v Baxendale, the ordinary £4,000 profit arises naturally from late delivery of commercial catering equipment to a caterer and is recoverable, as with the ordinary profits in Victoria Laundry. The £20,000 wedding contract is exceptional, and Ovenco had no knowledge of it, so it falls outside the second limb and is too remote, as with the lucrative dyeing contracts in Victoria Laundry. Dina must also have taken reasonable steps to mitigate, for example by hiring an oven if possible.

Conclusion. Dina probably has a s2(1) claim and a claim for late delivery recovering about £4,000 in lost profits plus any losses from the oven's lower capacity, provided the exclusion clause fails the reasonableness test, which is likely. She cannot recover the £20,000.

questions.q: Essay question. 'The decision in Williams v Roffey Bros has left the doctrine of consideration incoherent: the law enforces a promise to pay more but not a promise to accept less.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains the bargain theory of consideration and the existing duty rule (Stilk v Myrick; Hartley v Ponsonby)
Analyses Williams v Roffey: practical benefit, no duress; rationale of commercial reality and protecting genuine renegotiation
Explains Foakes v Beer and Pinnel's Case; Re Selectmove refusing to extend Roffey to part payment
Evaluates the asymmetry: arguments that practical benefit also exists in part payment (Lord Blackburn's doubts in Foakes)
Considers MWB v Rock (UKSC 2018) leaving the issue open and the role of promissory estoppel (High Trees; D & C Builders)
Discusses economic duress as the better tool to police variations, and reform/alternative views (e.g. abolition of consideration for variations)
Reaches a reasoned conclusion with clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement identifies a real tension. Consideration reflects the idea that English law enforces bargains: each side must give something for the other's promise. Traditionally, performing a duty you already owe the promisor is not consideration, so in Stilk v Myrick (1809) sailors could not enforce a promise of extra wages for completing the voyage, though in Hartley v Ponsonby (1857) going beyond the original duty was enough.

Williams v Roffey Bros [1991] changed this for promises to pay more. A main contractor promised a carpentry subcontractor additional payment per flat completed. The Court of Appeal held that the promise was enforceable because the contractor obtained a practical benefit, avoiding a penalty under the main contract and the trouble of finding a replacement, and because there was no economic duress or fraud. The court presented this as a refinement of Stilk rather than overruling it. The reasoning reflects commercial reality: businesses often renegotiate when difficulties arise, and the law should enforce freely agreed variations, while economic duress now polices extortion.

By contrast, promises to accept less remain governed by Foakes v Beer (1884), applying Pinnel's Case (1602): paying part of a debt is not consideration for forgoing the rest. In Re Selectmove [1995] the Court of Appeal refused to apply Roffey to part payment, because only the House of Lords could depart from Foakes. Yet a creditor who accepts part payment often obtains a practical benefit: certain receipt of some money and avoiding the cost and risk of enforcement. Lord Blackburn made a similar point in Foakes itself before reluctantly concurring. The distinction between 'more for the same' and 'the same for less' is therefore hard to justify on principle, which supports the claim of incoherence.

The Supreme Court had a chance to resolve this in MWB Business Exchange Centres v Rock Advertising [2018] but decided the case on the no-oral-modification clause and declined to rule on the consideration point, leaving the tension in place. In practice, the gap is partly filled by promissory estoppel: following High Trees [1947], a creditor who promises to accept less may be prevented from going back on that promise where the debtor relied on it and it would be inequitable. But estoppel is a limited fix. It is only a shield (Combe v Combe), is often suspensory, and depends on the debtor having acted equitably (D & C Builders v Rees).

Some argue the incoherence is defensible: Foakes protects creditors from pressure to accept less, a particular risk for small businesses. But economic duress, as developed in Atlas Express v Kafco and The Universe Sentinel, already addresses illegitimate pressure in both directions. A more coherent position would treat all genuine variations alike, enforcing them unless obtained by duress, either through a broad view of practical benefit or by dispensing with consideration for variations altogether.

In conclusion, the statement is largely correct. Roffey made consideration more flexible for increases while Foakes keeps it rigid for decreases, and the courts have so far declined to reconcile the two. Until the Supreme Court addresses the point directly, promissory estoppel and economic duress do much of the practical work, but they cannot remove the doctrinal inconsistency.
